Among the most important questions were the status of a Muslim who commits a major sin, the relationship between reason and faith, the meaning of justice in Islam, the proper attitude toward an unjust ruler, the duty to command what is right and forbid what is wrong, and the meaning of God’s transcendence and unity.

For decades after the question of divine decree first appeared, discussions of these issues remained scattered across several different fields. They appeared in works of jurisprudence and legal theory, and sometimes in philosophy, Sufism, and natural science. They had no clearly defined identity as a separate discipline and no systematic connection with one another.
Eventually, Arab thought reached a stage at which it was able to define and distinguish them more clearly.
At that point, these scattered discussions passed from a state of gradual quantitative accumulation into a distinct new form. They were classified as an independent field called kalām.

This meant that they had entered the broader stage of scientific classification that Arab thought as a whole was then beginning to reach. This was a genuinely advanced stage. Before it, the basic boundaries between different fields of knowledge were often unclear. The lines between jurisprudence, legal theory, and the foundations of religion could easily blur, as could those between grammar, rhetoric, and literature, or between Hadith, Qurʾanic commentary, history, and biography.
The reason was simple: each field had not yet developed its own clear boundaries, concepts, and categories.

This explains why the term ʿilm al-kalām appeared relatively late. It did not become common in books, debates, and intellectual struggles until the age of al-Maʾmūn, around the end of the second and beginning of the third Islamic centuries—that is, the ninth century CE.
We think the name ʿilm al-kalām became a formal term for this newly independent field because it gave a fixed name to an ordinary expression people had already been using informally.
When they discussed one of the questions that would later belong to this field, they often described what they were doing simply as kalām—“talk” or “discussion.”
We can see an example in a passage quoted by Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr (d. 463 AH/1070 CE):

Muṣʿab ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Zubayrī reported that Mālik ibn Anas used to say: “I dislike discussion about religion. The people of our city have always disliked it and warned against it—discussion of Jahm’s views, divine decree, and similar matters. I approve only of discussion concerning matters on which lawful action depends.”

Abū ʿUmar said: “Mālik, may God have mercy on him, has made clear that discussion of matters connected with action was permitted in his view and in the view of the scholars of his city. He also tells us that by ‘discussion about religion’ he meant such matters as the views of Jahm, divine decree, and so on.”
In this passage, the word kalām is used repeatedly for discussion of questions of religious belief—the same questions that later came to make up the field of kalām.

Before it became a technical term, however, the word was still being used in its ordinary linguistic sense of “speech” or “discussion.” Because it appeared so often when people spoke about what would later be called theological questions, the formal term ʿilm al-kalām eventually emerged during the period of classification as a fixed name for this already familiar usage.
Historical evidence shows that Arabs began systematically recording knowledge and writing books during the first Islamic century, the seventh century CE.

This means that writing about questions later associated with kalām must also have begun during that period. After all, the most important intellectual questions debated from the second half of that century onward—and the questions around which sectarian and ideological battles became most intense—were precisely those concerning human freedom of action, followed by questions of justice, God’s attributes, the meaning of faith and its relationship to reason, the status of a Muslim who commits a major sin, and so on.
All of these later became questions belonging to the field called kalām.

The logic of the situation therefore strongly suggests—if it does not make it almost certain—that more was written about these questions, which occupied nearly the whole intellectual life of first-century Islamic society, than about many other subjects.

Unfortunately, almost none of the works on kalām written during that period, and especially none of the Muʿtazilite works, survived even into the age immediately following it: the Abbasid period. If they had survived that long, we would surely have received at least some Umayyad writings on kalām and logic through Abbasid sources.
This historical fact raises an obvious question: why were these works lost?

We think the reason may be that Muʿtazilite thought at the time was especially productive, widespread, and attractive to the people of its society, precisely because, as we have already said, it challenged official Umayyad ideology more strongly than other currents did.

It is therefore quite possible that the political authorities of the time, together with the intellectual groups that supported them, worked to suppress this body of thought and perhaps even destroy it. As a result, most of what we know about it comes from the writings of its opponents.

After the middle of the second Islamic century, the eighth century CE—and especially from the reign of al-Maʾmūn onward—the writing of works on kalām expanded enormously. It would hardly be an exaggeration to say that books on kalām, together with the intellectual battles they provoked, became the most visible feature of intellectual life at the time.
This continued until philosophy emerged as a field separate from kalām, and indeed as something standing opposite it: a new and more advanced kind of ideological weapon.

The main source of this remarkable growth in writing on kalām was the increasingly intense struggle between the two camps that came to dominate almost the entire field: the Muʿtazila and the Ashʿarites. We will return to this later.
What are its main features and methods? What concepts distinguish it? What are its basic principles?

And who were the Muslim mutakallimūn, the practitioners of kalām? Were they only the Muʿtazila? Only the Ashʿarites? The Muʿtazila and Ashʿarites together, but no one else? Or should we also include the Shiʿa, Kharijites, Murjiʾa, and others?
How can we answer these questions scientifically, on the basis of historical documents and sources?

The first thing a researcher naturally does when trying to find an answer is to turn to definitions of the field given by scholars who belonged to it, historians who wrote about it, and later researchers.

In principle, the definition of any field should help us identify exactly what that field is, because a definition is supposed to state its essential features in the most precise and concentrated form.
Unfortunately, the surviving definitions of kalām do not do this.
The earliest definition that has reached us comes from Abū Naṣr al-Fārābī. His definition of the “art of kalām” says only that it is:
“a faculty by which a person can defend the particular beliefs and actions proclaimed by the founder of a religion, and refute through argument anything that opposes them.”
This does almost nothing to answer the questions before us.

It tells us only the purpose of kalām: to defend the beliefs and practices laid down by the religious lawgiver. It tells us nothing at all about the field’s basic structure, foundations, or general principles.

Immediately after this definition, however, al-Fārābī discusses two further points. First, he distinguishes jurisprudence from kalām. Second, he describes the different “methods and opinions by which religions are to be defended.”

For al-Fārābī, the essential difference between jurisprudence and kalām is this: the jurist takes the beliefs and actions laid down by the religious lawgiver as accepted foundations and then uses them to derive further rulings. The theologian’s task is simply to defend the very principles that the jurist takes for granted.
Al-Fārābī then explains how such a defense might be carried out.
But he does not present one specific method of kalām. Instead, he describes four different “methods” used by four groups of theologians, without telling us which one he himself accepts.
The first is the method of those who reject reason as a means of defending religious beliefs.

The second is the method of those who compare these beliefs with what is known through the senses, what is commonly accepted, and what reason establishes. If the beliefs agree with these, they use that agreement to defend them.
If there is a contradiction, they try to interpret the wording of the religious beliefs in a way that removes the conflict.

If interpretation cannot solve the problem, they try instead to challenge the sensory evidence, commonly accepted opinions, or rational conclusions and reinterpret them so that they agree with the religious beliefs.
If these forms of evidence themselves conflict with one another, they accept whichever ones agree with the religious beliefs and reject the others.

Finally, if none of these methods works and the contradiction remains between the religious beliefs on one side and sensory evidence, accepted opinion, or rational judgment on the other, then the religious beliefs must simply be accepted as the truth and defended on that basis.
The third method is to search other religions for every objectionable or scandalous feature that can be used to attack and discredit them. In this way, its followers defend their own religion.

The fourth is the method of those who defend their religion by making it appear attractive to others by whatever means happen to work—even if this requires “lying, sophistry, slander, and sheer stubbornness.”
So al-Fārābī gives us little more than a vague general description that defines almost nothing.
There is another problem as well. His treatment of theological method does not give the Muʿtazila their proper place among the theologians.
Where exactly are the Muʿtazila in al-Fārābī’s picture?
Perhaps they belong among the followers of the second method. But if so, the picture is unstable and incomplete. It does not clearly show the full character of their rationalist position.
In al-Fārābī’s account—if the Muʿtazila are indeed the group he means—they ultimately reject the judgment of reason whenever they cannot reconcile it with the meaning of the religious text.
But is this really an accurate description of the Muʿtazila?

One of the first things we know about them is that they developed a concept of faith radically different from that held by most Muslims. For them, knowledge and understanding were essential parts of faith itself.
This means that a faith not based on knowledge and understanding—on rational conviction—could not count as genuine faith.

The Muʿtazila also held that good and evil can be known by reason. In other words, whether something is good or evil exists objectively in the thing itself and does not depend on whether the religious lawgiver commands or forbids it.
A command to do one thing and a prohibition against another simply confirm the goodness or evil already present objectively in them.
Reason can recognize this objective reality on its own, even without knowing whether the religious lawgiver has commanded or forbidden the act.

This is why the Muʿtazila described good and evil as rational. They also described them as intrinsic, meaning that their goodness or evil exists objectively in the thing itself and does not come from outside it—that is, it does not come from the commands and prohibitions of religious law.

Taken together, these positions on faith and on rationally knowable good and evil show that reason occupies a much higher and firmer place in Muʿtazilite thought than it does among the followers of al-Fārābī’s second theological method.

If reason had held no greater place among the Muʿtazila than al-Fārābī’s account suggests, Sunni opposition to them would have been far less intense than the history of intellectual conflict shows it to have been from the birth of the movement down to the present day.
Yes, because even contemporary researchers sometimes write about the Muʿtazila with a hostility no less severe than that of their ancient enemies.
Al-Fārābī’s picture of the second theological method ultimately makes the religious text the final judge.

But both the historical record of Muʿtazilite thought and the surviving documents of that thought show something different. For the Muʿtazila, reason is the judge when dealing with ambiguous Qurʾanic verses. It is also the judge when evaluating prophetic Hadith: if a report conflicts with reason and cannot be interpreted in a rationally acceptable way, they reject it as inauthentic.

Even so, despite our criticism of al-Fārābī’s definition of kalām and despite the unclear place of the Muʿtazila in his account of its methods, his discussion does give us something important that we do not find in the other definitions available to us.
His account includes several different theological schools and methods.
From this, we learn that kalām did not belong to one Muslim school alone. It was an intellectual and ideological field shared by several schools and groups.
Other definitions take the opposite approach. They restrict kalām either to the Ashʿarites or to the Muʿtazila.
Very few original Muʿtazilite texts have reached us directly. They are, in fact, extremely rare. On this particular question, we have found only one passage, by al-Khayyāṭ, who says:
“You should know that kalām belongs to them”—meaning the Muʿtazila—“and to no one else.”

The remaining definitions are Ashʿarite. In all of them, kalām appears as a purely Ashʿarite discipline, as if the Muʿtazila had never had anything to do with it, and as if no group outside the Sunnis had ever taken part in it.
Consider, for example, Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī’s explanation of the “purpose of kalām”:

“Its purpose is to preserve the creed of the Sunnis and protect it from the confusion introduced by the people of innovation. (...) Then Satan planted in the minds of the innovators ideas that contradicted the Sunna. They became absorbed in them and came close to disturbing the true belief of its followers. So God raised up a group of theologians and moved them to defend the Sunna through ordered argument, exposing the deceptions of the new innovators who opposed the inherited teaching of the Sunnis. From this arose kalām and its practitioners, and so on.”
If we take al-Ghazālī’s words at face value, then the history of kalām begins only when Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī founded his school in opposition to the Muʿtazila.
Everything the Muʿtazila had written and debated in the field before that point would then have to be erased from the history of kalām.
Ibn Khaldūn follows the same path in his definition. He begins:
“Kalām is a field of knowledge that argues for the beliefs of faith through rational proofs and refutes innovators who depart in their beliefs from the doctrines of the early Muslims and the Sunnis.”

As he explains this definition, it becomes clear that by “innovators who depart in their beliefs from the doctrines of the early Muslims and the Sunnis,” he means the Shiʿa, Murjiʾa, anthropomorphists, Muʿtazila, and Imamis.

He then says that the innovations of these groups and schools created the need “to defend these beliefs with rational proofs against the attacks of these innovations,” and that “Shaykh Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī, the imam of the theologians, undertook this task,” and so on.

Ibn Khaldūn then reviews the questions al-Ashʿarī addressed in his response to these “innovators and deviants,” and concludes that after the question of the imamate had been added, the whole collection of these questions came to be called kalām.
There can therefore be little doubt that among the Ashʿarites, the term kalām had a particular meaning and a particular content that applied only to Ashʿarite theology.
The same was true of the term mutakallimūn, “theologians,” which was likewise restricted to Ashʿarite theologians.
This removes from the history of kalām all the rational thought based on philosophical reflection that appeared before Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī.

It also excludes all the creative rationalist theologians of that earlier period who helped prepare the way for Arab-Islamic philosophy. At an early stage in its intellectual awakening, they trained Arab-Islamic thought to work with abstraction, concepts, and categories.
We have no objection to the Ashʿarites choosing whatever names and terms they wish for their own school and their own thought.
But we do object when they cut away part of the history of kalām so completely that the field appears to begin and end with them.
We should therefore set aside the claims of both the Muʿtazila and the Ashʿarites that kalām belongs exclusively within the boundaries of their own particular school.
Instead, we must look at history and historical reality as they actually developed, in all their dimensions.

If we do this, and follow the long history of kalām from Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ (d. 131 AH/748 CE), the founder of the Muʿtazilite school, to Ibn Taymiyya (661–728 AH/thirteenth–fourteenth centuries CE), one of the best-known later traditionalist theologians, two basic conclusions emerge.

First, kalām includes the whole range of questions framed in religious and doctrinal terms that arose from different forms of social and political conflict in Arab-Islamic society from the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs onward.

Over time, these questions were transformed into complex ideas about the world beyond nature. Their original social dimensions became almost hidden behind a fog of abstractions. Alongside these appeared views with a philosophical direction concerning the natural world, though still approached from a theological point of view.
Many different schools and tendencies of kalām appeared during this long history. Yet the basic questions they discussed and disputed remained largely the same.

And if we look beyond the outward form of the ideas, the deepest reasons for disagreement over each of these questions—whether individually or as a whole—were always rooted in social reality. At their deepest level, they arose from the position occupied by the supporters of these ideas within the wider social structure of their society.
Second, kalām passed through two main stages during this history of roughly six centuries: a Muʿtazilite stage and an Ashʿarite stage.
